steps.body:
On [0, 2π), sin x = 1/2 gave two solutions (recall the twins π/6 and 5π/6). But sine repeats every 2π forever, so EVERY solution is one of those two **plus any whole number of turns**:

x = π/6 + 2πk or x = 5π/6 + 2πk, k any integer.

Two families capture infinitely many answers.
Why the answers come in families.

widget.prompt: Rotate to 150°. Then keep going a full turn and watch what happens to the coordinates.
widget.successFeedback: At 150° the coordinates are fixed — and a full turn later, at 510°, they are exactly the same point. That is why every trig equation has infinitely many solutions: the circle does not remember how many laps you took. The +2πk is the lap counter.
widget.lowFeedback: Not far enough round — 150° sits between 90° and 180°.

predict.prompt: When the point moves to 90°, which coordinate becomes 1?
predict.reveal: At 90°, the unit-circle point is (0,1), so sine is 1 and cosine is 0. The horizontal coordinate can't be the 1: at 90° the point sits straight up on the y-axis, so its x-coordinate — cosine — has shrunk all the way to 0.

cml.actionGoal: Move the angle and coordinate the circle point, triangle ratios, and trigonometric values.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Change the controlling quantity in this unitCircleExplore away from the successful state. Which invariant remains true, and which visible consequence changes?

explanation.prompt: Why are cosine and sine the point's coordinates?

options.label: They are the horizontal and vertical projections of a radius of length one.
options.feedback: Exactly—this identifies the governing mechanism rather than only the final pattern.

options.label: They are arbitrary labels attached to the axes.
options.feedback: That describes an appearance or shortcut, not the invariant that makes the relationship hold.

options.label: They both equal the arc length.
options.feedback: The live model contradicts that claim when its control is changed.

explanationVariants: k = −1 gives π/6 − 2π = −11π/6 ≈ −5.76 — negative angles are members too; sin(−11π/6) = 1/2 ✓.
The ladder runs both directions: every integer k, including negatives.

widget.prompt: Which value belongs to the family x = π/6 + 2πk?

options.label: π/6 − 2π (k = −1)
options.feedback: Right — negative k just spins backwards; the sine is still 1/2 there.

options.label: π/6 + π
options.feedback: Adding HALF a turn lands at 7π/6, where sin = −1/2. The family steps by FULL turns 2π.

options.label: 5π/6
options.feedback: 5π/6 solves the equation but belongs to the OTHER family (5π/6 + 2πk) — the twin, not this ladder.

steps.body: Why two families and not one? Because 2π-stepping from π/6 never reaches 5π/6 (they differ by 2π/3, not a multiple of 2π). The complete answer is always: **each [0, 2π) solution founds its own +2πk family**. Same recipe for cosine with its twins x₁ and 2π − x₁.

explanationVariants: Each of the 2 families contributes one member per full turn; [0, 6π) holds 3 turns: 2 × 3 = 6 solutions.
List them: π/6, 5π/6, then +2π: 13π/6, 17π/6, then +4π: 25π/6, 29π/6 — six.

widget.prompt: How many solutions does sin x = 1/2 have on [0, 6π)?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is the count in ONE turn [0, 2π). Three turns triple it: 6.
Each turn contributes TWO (the twins), not one: 3 turns × 2 = 6.

explanationVariants: cos x = 1/2: base solutions π/3 and 5π/3 (recall 2π − π/3); each grows a +2πk family.
Two families from the two [0, 2π) twins, stepped by full turns.

widget.prompt: The GENERAL solution of cos x = 1/2 is:

options.label: x = π/3 + 2πk or x = 5π/3 + 2πk
options.feedback: Right — cosine's twin pair (x₁ and 2π − x₁), each carrying its own 2πk ladder.

options.label: x = π/3 + 2πk only
options.feedback: That misses half the answers — 5π/3, 11π/3, … all have cosine 1/2 too. Two families.

options.label: x = π/3 + πk
options.feedback: Stepping by π flips the sign every step: π/3 + π = 4π/3 has cosine −1/2. Full turns only: 2πk, two families.

steps.body: Pick the members in a window.
explanationVariants: Families π/6 + 2πk and 5π/6 + 2πk intersected with [2π, 4π): 13π/6 and 17π/6 — their sum is 30π/6 = 5π ≈ 15.71.
One member from each family lands in the third turn: 13π/6 ≈ 6.81 and 17π/6 ≈ 8.90; sum ≈ 15.71.
hints: Add 2π to each base solution π/6 and 5π/6.

widget.prompt: Sum the solutions of sin x = 1/2 that lie in [2π, 4π), to hundredths.

commonErrors.feedback: π is the sum of the BASE pair π/6 + 5π/6. Each gained 2π in this window: total π + 4π = 5π ≈ 15.71.
6.81 is just 13π/6, one member. Add its twin 17π/6 ≈ 8.90: ≈ 15.71.

takeaways: k ranges over ALL integers, negatives included.
Solutions per window = (families) × (turns in the window).
steps.teaser: Next: tangent's ladder is twice as dense — and one family suffices.

concept.body: Recipe: solve on [0, 2π) via the twins (recall), then append +2πk to EACH solution. Never merge distinct twins into one family.

explanationVariants: 17π/6 = 5π/6 + 2π: a k = 1 member of the 5π/6 family; sin(17π/6) = 1/2 ✓.
Subtract full turns until you land in [0, 2π): 17π/6 − 2π = 5π/6, a base solution.

widget.prompt: Is 17π/6 a solution of sin x = 1/2?

options.label: Yes — it's 5π/6 + 2π
options.feedback: Right — strip one full turn and the base twin appears.

options.label: No — it's bigger than 2π
options.feedback: Solutions live beyond [0, 2π) too — that's the whole point of +2πk. 17π/6 − 2π = 5π/6 ✓.

options.label: No — sin(17π/6) = −1/2
options.feedback: 17π/6 is one FULL turn past 5π/6, so the sine is unchanged: +1/2.
